props.title: My Last Round

sections.content: **My Last Round** (2011) stands as a powerful Chilean drama that masterfully interweaves LGBTQ+ themes with the gritty world of boxing. Director Julio Jorquera Arriagada creates an intimate portrait that echoes the emotional complexity of Weekend (2011) and the sporting intensity of The Fighter (2010). The film's exploration of masculinity in Latin American culture shares DNA with other groundbreaking queer cinema like **Bad Hair** (2013) and **XXY** (2007), while its boxing elements recall the raw authenticity of **Girlfight** (2000).

sections.content: The film's protagonist, Octavio, a middle-aged boxing trainer who falls in love with Hugo, a young kitchen worker, represents a departure from traditional sports drama narratives. Their relationship develops against the backdrop of Chile's conservative society, reminiscent of the social tensions in A Fantastic Woman (2017) and the forbidden love portrayed in **Happy Together** (1997). The boxing sequences, while less stylized than mainstream films like **Creed** (2015), carry a raw authenticity that amplifies the story's emotional impact.

The film's handling of health issues and athletic ambition parallels other sports dramas like **Million Dollar Baby** (2004) and The Wrestler (2008), but with a distinctive Latin American perspective. Director Arriagada's intimate camera work and naturalistic approach shares stylistic elements with contemporary Chilean cinema like **Gloria** (2013) and **No** (2012). sections.content: **My Last Round** (2011) subverts traditional sports movie tropes by focusing on the peripheral figure of the trainer rather than the boxer, similar to how **Warrior** (2011) explored family dynamics through MMA. The film's exploration of age differences and power dynamics in relationships recalls elements from **Pain and Glory** (2019) and **God's Own Country** (2017), while maintaining its unique perspective on Chilean masculinity and sexuality.
